utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Just before we start, Mr. Milovancevic, I just wanted to say to you that the Chamber has reconsidered its comments yesterday about the one set time, and it has decided to let you drive your own case and your own time but will give you the overall time that you are allowed for the Defence in a revised 73 ter schedule that will be handed down some time today. May the witness please make the oath, or make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. The examination-in-chief will be led by my co-counsel, Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Before we begin the examination-in-chief that I will be conducting as a member of the Defence team of Mr. Martic, I have to I have two request questions to make to you. First of all, I will try to put brief questions and I will appreciate brief answers. We will save time that way. That is one. And the second caution I would like to make has to do with interpretation. It is important to record your words and mine precisely, and for that to happen, it is necessary to make a brief pause before you begin to answer. And I hope we will both be able to take care of that. I hope we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If my learned friend from the Prosecution does not object, I would like to lead you through your CV and, if necessary, you will correct me if I am wrong or make whatever additions you see fitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Black, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you were born in 1944?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In a place called Budacka Rijeka in the then Republic of Croatia, that is in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You completed your primary school in Gornji Budacki, that's the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From 1961 to 1963 you attended a school for NCOs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After which you were transferred to a garrison in Pec?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From 1963 to 1968, you attended the military academy in Belgrade, the section of ground forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After completing the military academy, you stayed in Virovitica as company commander, then platoon commander, and assistant battalion commander for morale and training?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From 1975 to 1977, you attended the higher political school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from this school, you served in Podravska Slatina as assistant commander and then commander of the border section.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1980, you were transferred to Virovitica where you served in the following posts: Assistant commander of the mixed anti-armour artillery brigade for morale, and later commander of the border battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1986, you were transferred, again, in the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel then, to Zagreb to the command of the 5th Army District?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said you were born in a place called Budacka Rijeka. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Perovic, what is the witnesses name? You have just addressed him as Mr. Peric, but we would like to get his full names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there was a little confusion at the beginning. The witness's name is Slobodan Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Confirm that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. My name is Slobodan Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you are Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The village where you were born, Budacka Rijeka, was it an exclusively Serb village or was it mixed in population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It was exclusively Serb. There were no members of other ethnic groups in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When I ask you this, I mean the time you were born.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: When I was born, yes, there was one family by the name of Jasnic, Marica Jasnic at the end of the village. They had a house and that was the only mixed family. He was Serb and she was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So we can say that it was an exclusively Serb village with a single Croat house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just take a second before you begin to answer me, please. You were born in 1944. So during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about what happened in your village during the Second World War? Very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, I can say that my village is 60 kilometres away from Zagreb. It lived through unprecedented terror inflicted by the Croatian army at the time, it was almost bat down and more than half of the inhabitants were killed, had their throats slit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was any of your immediate family killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. From my immediate family, my grandfather, Novak, that is my paternal grandfather, had his throat cut, along with another 103 inhabitants in the St. Petka church near Vojnic on the 29th April, 1942. Whereas my grandmother, Kata, was burned in the concentration camp of Jasenovac, in an oven, in a furnace that had a particular name. My uncle, Andrija, was killed in a column of refugees in Biljeg. And there were many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From your CV, we saw that from 1968 to 1986 as an uncommissioned officer of the JNA and later officer you served in Virovitica, Podravska Slatina and again in Virovitica. In which former Yugoslav republic are these places located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In the former Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So in your entire military career, you served practically only in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What were the intra-ethnic relations like in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: You mean within the Yugoslav People's Army or in society as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I mean in society as a whole, because that must have been a code by relations within the army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, to be very brief, until 1980, of the last century so to speak, there was -- those relations were dominated by tolerance and there were no major incidents, except in 1971 and the rise of Croatian nationalism in what was known as maspok. And then again in 1980, those relations were, again, disrupted by rising intolerance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the beginning of the 1970s and the rise of the nationalist movement in Croatia called the mass movement, or maspok in our language. What were the sources of that movement? Very briefly. Just let me ask you one more thing in this connection. At that time, you were serving in the Virovitica garrison; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So tell us what you know about that period, as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Forces emerged onto the socio-political scene at the time that were opposed to the communist party and the socialist order of Croatia at the time. Croatia was one of the main centres -- sorry, Virovitica was one of the main centres of this nationalist movement, and there was this mass rally in Virovitica with a large crowd of people walking from Vocin to Podravska Slatina to Virovitica in 1971. And they had certain demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1971?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was assistant commander for logistics in the 5th Army District at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I do remember the commander of the district was Djoko Jovanic, and his assistant for logistics was General Janko Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So in 1971, at the time of the rising nationalism in Croatia, the assistant commander for logistics in the 5th Army District was General Janko Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what were the principal ideas of this maspok movement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The platform of the maspok, the political platform, was dominated by some main ideas primarily that Croatia should be independent, that it should acquire elements of statehood, become a member of state of the United Nations because allegedly it was being exploited by the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember some of the main protagonists on the political scene who belonged to this maspok movement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: There were many of them. Savka Dapcevic-Kucar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to enumerate more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are requested to be a little slower. The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters are not able to keep pace with you, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And if you allow me, I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember some of the main protagonists who reappeared again in the political arena, later in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, from those that I enumerated, Savka Dapcevic-Kucar, Mika Tripalo. There was Drazen Budisa, Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, Sime Dzodan. Sime Dzodan was one of the most extreme members. That's it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, in those years, in the 1970s and more precisely in 1971, what was the role of Tudjman, Bobetko and Vladimir Seks? What was their role in the maspok movement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I remember Tudjman was not the foremost among them. He kept a lower profile. He probably didn't have enough courage to take a leading role, so they were saving him. And Bobetko -- sorry, Tudjman was then a retired general. I think he was employed by some institute in Zagreb, some historical institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Those people that I mentioned, Tudjman, Bobetko, Seks and others, were they convicted later after the political defeat of the maspok movement and why?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I know Mesic was convicted; he served his sentence in Stara Gradiska. I know Vladimir Seks was convicted as well. And Tudjman as well, but I don't think he served much of his sentence. I think he was later paroled and I think Tito himself pardoned him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And why were they convicted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For disrupting the integrity of the state union and aspirations to undermine the state with their separatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So I'm reminding everyone again, this was year 1971?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1986 you were transferred to the command of the 5th Army District in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your specific duty at the headquarters or the command of the 5th Army District, what were you tasked with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the main department, which was the operations and training department of the command of the 5th Army District. I was, among other things, tasked with border affairs, state border affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, your concrete duty had to do with the control of the Yugoslav border? Opposite whose borders; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I had 888 kilometres of state border under my purview, which came within the area of responsibility of the 5th Army District from Ankaran all the way down to Donji Miholjac, that is the border opposite Italy, Austria and Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time you were transferred to the command of the 5th Army District in Zagreb, who was the commander of the 5th Army District; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: At the time of my transfer, the army commander was Colonel General Martin Spegelj who had been holding that position for a year, before my transfer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was General Spegelj's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us of the state of affairs of the situation in the 5th Army District of the JNA in the period when General Spegelj was the commander thereof?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific with regard to the time period? And in what sense do you mean "the state of affairs"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was characteristic of the time of his command over the district?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I can speak from my personal experience at the time I carried out my duties there on the basis of official and unofficial meetings with General Spegelj and on the basis of the orders he issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I had in mind. I wanted to hear what you personally knew and on the basis of your personal knowledge, how would you characterise the period during which Spegelj was at the head of the 5th Army District?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Let me be specific: I had been trained in the Tito's army and until Spegelj arrived there and took this position, I never paid attention to persons' ethnicities, whether they were Serb, Croat, Slovene, and perhaps only by their names I would notice their ethnicity. In this period, the human resources or personnel policy applied in the JNA changed in a way that puzzled me. For instance, at the time I was commander in Virovitica in 1985, before my transfer in 1986, Spegelj became commander and started insisting that civilians who had served the military service and who hailed from his hometown and who held the rank of lance-corporal to be admitted into the army on the basis of three-year contracts with the possibility of extending the contract twice for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there. You said that Martin Spegelj insisted that the ranks be filled by people from his hometown in the area. What was the ethnicity of these people that he insisted on having admitted into the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Whose decision was it as to who would form the commanding staff of the 5th Army District at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the position of a commander? Of army commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I meant the persons who were General Spegelj's subordinates.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it was the commander himself who decided about this. At his staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the commander was Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was General Spegelj most governed by in deciding who to appoint to the position of chiefs of departments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In this area and a comprehensive reorganisation of the command also took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just be brief, please, Mr. Peric. What was General Spegelj governed by in making his choices?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: He took care to appoint Croat, Slovene or Muslim officers to these positions in order to reduce the number of Serb officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you follow subsequent, the subsequent career of General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What became of him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: He became a member of the HDZ party, and although he had initially run as a candidate of the Racan's SDP, he ultimately joined the HDZ and became the minister of defence. Later on, due to some rivalries among their ranks, he was -- he fell out of their mercy, but at any rate, he managed to survive on the Croatian political scene. I omitted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: When he was retired after the elections in May 1991, he established a Croatian army. The Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Before the Croatian army was established, do you recall anything that was specific of General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, the illicit importing of weapons, which was done by Cazmatrans trailer trucks across the Hungarian border, Terelino Polje, at Gorican, these were the border crossings. The Cazmatrans trailer trucks imported weapons from Hungary and he was the main organiser of this exercise. My superior officer, Captain Jagar, made a film about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This film was publicised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was broadcast I believe on the 26th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You had occasion to view the film?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Captain Jagar, did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I admitted him into the service to be the commander of the border watch-tower, and it was actually Spegelj who took Jagar to his army headquarters to be the head of the training grounds, because he hailed 6 from his hometown.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This same person, Jagar, filmed this clip, and in the film he and Spegelj were the protagonists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you knew Captain Jagar personally, did you at any point doubt the authenticity of the film after having viewed it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No, not once, because I was familiar with the facilities where the film was shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOPEFUL
utterances.text: Excuse me, how do you spell the name Jagar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How it is that one spells the family name Jagar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is Vlado, V-l-a-d-o, and his last name J-a-g-a-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOPEFUL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that your duty was to control the Yugoslav border opposite Italy, Austria and Hungary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like at the border in the period you served in Zagreb? Did anything change at that time? You spoke of the illicit supply of weapons.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few changes. Since I was in charge of the border, I compiled monthly reports for the General Staff in Belgrade. I received information from subordinate commands. There were ten border battalions in all. I received information, in particular, about Croatia, that's to say the area called Podravina opposite the Hungarian border, that civilians were spotted carrying weapons in the villages of Novaki, Predrijevo [phoen], Laska. I repeat, it was from the subordinated commands, especially from Podravina, Virovitica and Koprivnica where the commands of the border battalions were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Are these places opposite the Hungarian border?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received their reports signed by the commanders of these border battalions to the effect that in the places in the general area of Virovitica, Sopje, Vaska, Novaki, in the area of Koprivnica, Golaz, Dalam, civilians, Croats were spotted with weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Which year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, between 1987 and 1991, throughout that period. On the basis of these reports by my subordinates, I compiled a general report, an aggregate report for my command. The aggregated report, of course, was to be signed by the army commander, that's to say General Spegelj, or his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were transferred to Zagreb in 1986. How long did your service in Zagreb last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Until the 17th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, what was the area of responsibility of the 5th Army District?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 5th Army District encompassed practically the entire Slovenia, more than 50 percent of Croatia, the boundary was Knin, down there, and up here Slovanski Brod, and still further up, Orahovica. So basically two-thirds of Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this period of time, and we're talking about 1990, do you remember whether multi-party elections were held in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Elections were held in Slovenia where Demos won. There were elections in Croatia as well and the HDZ won them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After these elections, did there come a change in the attitude of Slovenia and Croatia towards the Yugoslav People's Army; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It all started at first with the mass media. It was followed by a boycott, which ultimately ended in the taking off of the boards which said "the Socialist Republic of Slovenia" and the replacement of them by the words "Republic of Slovenia."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We will talk about that a bit later. What I meant was whether there was a change in the attitude of Slovenia and Croatia vis-a-vis the JNA, their commanding officers and soldiers themselves. If there was indeed a change, what would you say was typical of them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The changes started with the interruption of the work of the 14th Congress and the walk-out of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In 1989. And it was at that point that the official authorities, as did the public at large, changed their attitude toward the JNA. This happened in Croatia later on. To put it simply, this feeling of togetherness disappeared, this artificial rift started to being created. They kept refusing various invitations to the federal organs and this divide grew bigger by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And after the HDZ won the elections in Croatia, what was its attitude toward the JNA an its organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Almost following the same pattern as had been seen in Slovenia, the events unfolded in Croatia, with the use of the same means, although in perhaps a more radical form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you say in a more radical form, what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I was speaking in terms of a full boycott and isolation of the JNA barracks, the cutting off of supplies of electricity, telephone lines, water. Later on in 1991 with the blockade of the JNA barracks, where they were fully isolated and under close supervision, leaflets were being distributed where it was said that children should not socialise with the children of the JNA personnel, that the JNA personnel was parking their vehicles in the places that constituted obstacles. There were derogatory terms used for the JNA, and the JNA had been the hot bed of the Yugoslav identity. They called us Yugoslav Chetnik units, and they used terms that were even worse than that. Dreadful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The first armed conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia took place in Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So very briefly what happened in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, they issued this unilateral act of secession, and, in effect, Slovenia moved to officially separate from Yugoslavia, and thus on the 25th of June, instead of hoardings saying the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the border, new hoardings appeared saying Republic of Slovenia. And we had an article in the constitution governing the border and border crossings which stipulated that border units of the army were in charge of providing -- of securing the border outside population centres and public roads; whereas on public roads and in population centres, the border shall be secured by members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Peric. So if I understood you correctly, and I stand to be corrected, Slovenia took over the state borders of Yugoslavia then, in end June 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, they placed their own police on the border crossings. They had customs officers of their own from before. But they placed new signs indicating that it was the independent Republic of Slovenia now, and they wouldn't let anybody from the federal authorities come and see what was going on at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did this conflict in Slovenia end?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Regrettably it ended in a way that none of us in the army wanted, and nobody among the people wanted it either, with a clash between the Slovene Territorial Defence and the Yugoslavia People's Army. They practically usurped the Territorial Defence which, according to the law, was a component of the armed forces of the federal Yugoslavia. However, they took over the TO and used it against the units of the Yugoslav People's Army who were charged with restoring the federal authority on the federal border.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time the only legitimate armed force in Yugoslavia was what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And there was no other?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This conflict was ended with a withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We're moving into leading questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic, you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that. I will rephrase. I accept that the way I put it a moment ago the question might have been leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Peric, there was a conflict. How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: From the 26th of June, 1991, until perhaps the 7th of July, when the decision was made to cease hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I think the federal Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And what then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: After their decision, the decision to withdraw the JNA from Slovenia followed soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the JNA units that had been stationed in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you very briefly. I think there are few armies in the world, especially in federal states, that would have allowed their personnel to be humiliated like the JNA did. I had soldiers, Slovenes, Croats, Albanians and others asking me: How come that so -- such educated people who had won the elections were capable of humiliating and insulting even young soldiers, 20 years their junior in such a way?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you for a very brief answer. What happened to the JNA units that had been stationed in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: First of all, they were placed under a blockade. Then they were attacked, both when they tried to approach the border and when they were withdrawing. To a lesser extent when they were withdrawing, but they were attacked when they tried to approach the border, and they tried because they had orders to take over control of the border, but without opening fire. They had orders not to open fire. The Slovene forces took advantage of this and they fired mercilessly at those children who were sitting ducks because they had orders not to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA finally withdraw from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it finally did. With part of its material and equipment and all of the personnel mostly using the Ljubljana-Zagreb-Belgrade road and parts of the JNA moved into Bosnia through Bihac, and part of the units moved along the shore towards Ploce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So while withdrawing from Slovenia with the materiel and equipment and personnel, they had to go via Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was equipment and personnel withdrawn from Slovenia without any problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: To the extent that I know, and I had to follow these developments through my work from a forward command post of the 5th Army District in Slunj, I monitored the withdrawal of JNA personnel and equipment from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On their way through Croatia, you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, not all the equipment could be transported by railway. Some of it had to go by road, and some of it via Rijeka to Montenegro, and part of the equipment stayed in Slovenia; for instance, in the area of Biograd Pijuk. Some armour equipment stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. All this equipment that was transported out of Slovenia, by rail, by road and otherwise, was it without hinderance and without problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No. All these convoys from the direction of Ljubljana, Maribor of the 31st and the 14th Corps, they were all intercepted and attacked. I know of four incidents when 25 rail-cars in one train were intercepted and robbed by the Croatian armed forces. Combat and non-combat equipment from those trains was removed and hidden in depth of the Croatian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now see the Defence Exhibit 106. Can we enlarge it a bit. Mr. Peric, can you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From the heading, can you see to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The command of the 9th Corps addressed this letter to the General Staff of the SFRY Yugoslavia and the command of the naval district in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: There must be a misunderstanding. This is not the exhibit I wanted to show you. I have -- my notes that this should be Exhibit 106. Defence Exhibit 1D0-106.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can help. It's a little confusing, because this is a 65 ter number the one that's been given and they just have a different format than the Prosecution ones. The ERN of this document, or the document ID should be 1D00-5073, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: 5071 actually in the B/C/S. 5073 is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have the right document. Now if we can only enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That is the document. Can you see it now, Mr. Peric? From the heading of this document, can you see to whom it was addressed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It comes from the office of the federal secretary, addressed to the prime minister of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Greguric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 of this document, just to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It's assistant federal secretary, Admiral Stane Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to page 1. And zoom in a little, please. Mr. Peric --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- could you please read the introduction and paragraph 1 of this letter.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "Mr. President, I hereby inform you of the unprecedented robbery of looting of military equipment committed by members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia on 29th August 1991." Paragraph 1. "On the railway, Zagreb Belgrade, in the village of Ivankovo, west of Vinkovci, a train carrying military equipment was intercepted. The train consisted of 29 freight and two passenger cars. The authorities of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia and members of the Home Guard Corps attacked the train, disarmed the crew, and took them we do not know where for the moment. All the military equipment was removed from the train that had been transported from the Republic of Slovenia following a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that -- is the information given here correct, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we have come to a convenient moment for the break, but can we please turn to this document before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much we will now take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You do remember where we left it off before the break. Let me ask you this: What was the situation like in Croatia in that time period? And we were talking about 1991 and the intercepting of the trains that were taking military equipment from Slovenia. Can you tell us, from your memory, what the situation was like in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The situation in Croatia at the time was as follows: The nature of my work took me to different parts of Croatia and led me to be in contact not only with the structures on the borders, but also with the local political authorities, with the local residents, the people, Croats and Serbs were growing fearful. Let me tell you that the population inhabiting the area around Hungarian and Croatian border, especially that of Slatina, had a sizeable Serb population; for instance, there was 7 -- 12 villages in that area where there was Serb population. The Serb population there grew ever more fearful because they noticed that the Croatian population, local population had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, did you have any information as to who had been arming the population and based on what criteria?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Already at that time peculiar things were happening in Croatia - I saw them peculiar as a military person - where the Croatian authorities usurped the military files that were kept in the secretariats for national defence, holding information about persons who were supposed to be recruited. These files were transferred to the TO and the best personnel were hired to man the structures of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why this was done?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, and later on this proved correct, the Croatian authorities tried and were successful in radically bringing up the levels of manpower of the MUP. Much higher than was normal for peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why this increase in the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, because they wanted to achieve some matters that in their view was impossible to achieve by peaceful means, to achieve them through violence. In addition to that, the legal supplies of weapons, especially through -- from Hungary, that were distributed to HDZ members and, in particular, to the local population along borders and close to military garrisons, which resulted in the formation of paramilitary units. However, this -- there was an attempt to conceal this effort from the federal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What did the federal bodies do, what steps did they take to prevent the process? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Through the regular flow of information that reached us, operations reports and such other information, I came to know that the federal Presidency had taken a decision to -- with regard to the weapons held by the illegal units outside the army itself, have it returned. Unfortunately, the Croatian authorities boycotted the decision, did not act upon it, and only a small percentage of the weapons was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This order of the federal secretariat for defence, did it also apply to the weapons held by the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was usurped by the Croatian authorities, in that they wanted to use them as their own armed force, rather than the force of the -- of Yugoslavia. Since there was the danger that the Croatian authorities would take the weapons from the TO, an order was issued that the weapons held in TO depots locally be transferred to the JNA facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was this order, in fact, carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, it was, but only partially. Basically to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the most drastic form of pressure exerted on the JNA and its facilities at this point in time, and we are speaking of the following period, summer and autumn of 1991. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The most drastic form of pressure was the calling on the professional military personnel and on the military servicemen, not only those of Croat ethnicity, but also those of Muslim, Macedonian, Albanian and even Serb ethnicities, to leave JNA units. Secondly, there was pressure brought to bear, especially on the professional personnel of Croat ethnicity, regardless of the fact that these officers or non-commissioned officers had sworn their allegiance to the JNA, in terms of them being called upon to leave JNA units. A good part of these commanding officers, senior officers like myself, were, in effect, hesitant, reluctant to leave the JNA as they had sworn in to the JNA, and nevertheless they left because they said, well, we have to. We don't have another homeland but that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: There were some events that took place in autumn 1991. What happened to the garrisons in the area of -- in the territory of Croatia, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Especially as of 23rd of August and then throughout September, and offensive was launched by Croatian paramilitary forces against what was at the time still a legal armed force, that's to say the JNA, against their units, garrisons facilities and property, especially those garrisons that contained heavy military hardware, and border watch-towers, border posts. Normally a blockade would first be imposed which would then be followed by an outright attack. The balance of power -- of powers was tipped because, let's say that a garrison holding some 200 soldiers would be attacked by 4.000 strong Croatian police who had a flying brigade, a mobile brigade that went from one barracks to another. They would launch an attack, a merciless attack against a barracks calling upon the JNA soldiers to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about end of August and September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: In this time period, do you recall whether there were any more drastic forms of treatment of the JNA personnel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. My successor who I transferred my duty to in Virovitica, Major Rade Vuckovic [phoen], was touring the border in Podravina along the line Virovitica-Slatina, what -- came under attack whilst he was in a vehicle by the so-called Menlaneva Group [phoen]. He came under gunfire and was wounded to his shoulder and three fingers of his right hand were injured. I believe this took place on the 11th of July. In July at any rate. The following day I went to see him in the hospital in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any other such drastic incidents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The incident involving the attack on the garrison in Belgrade in early September -- interpreter's correction, in Bjelovar where Colonel Kovacevic was killed as well as the chief of security, Captain Dragisa Jovanovic, they suffered more losses and ultimately the soldiers were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who carried out this attack against the garrison in Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian paramilitary formation so-called ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: So-called ZNG and MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other attacks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The garrison in Varazdin came under attack, as did the 288th Mixed Anti-Armour Brigade in Virovitica numbering some 200 men. They were attacked by 4.000 HDZ members, ZNG members and such-like men. There were some other smaller garrisons that came under attack. At any rate, this was a synchronised orchestrated action with the knowledge of and under the instructions of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Does the date of 21st of September, 1991, mean anything to the witness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I was at the forward command post at Slunj on that date, the 21st of September, and I received a report from 580th Brigade, the commander of which was Colonel Svetozar Marijanovic, and the brigade was stationed at Cerovac [phoen], south of Karlovac, to the effect that at the Korana bridge at the entrance to Karlovac from the direction of Kamensko, a massacre had been committed by the Croatian paramilitary forces where 13 members of the reserve forces of the JNA had been viciously killed. They were disarmed, forced to lie prone on the ground, and at that point they were mutilated, ran through by knives and so on and so forth. I received a report on this later that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a video clip and I will put several questions to you in connection with that. Do you have it on your screens? Can you follow, Mr. Peric? Mr. Peric, can you follow the clip?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop there. Stop the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I want to put a question to you. The men in uniform, who are they, in your view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore are they wearing olive-drab uniforms which were uniforms of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you conclude on the basis of what you've seen what they're doing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I think this is the footage from Krnjak, where they were taking over the bodies of those killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the community centre at Krnjak. My village is about four kilometres away from this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What we are looking at is the dead bodies of the JNA troops who had been killed at the Korana bridge are being taken away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, that might perhaps be a notorious fact, but you are leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do allow for that possibility, but the witness did say that he was familiar with the incident and that was why I said that what we were looking at was the bodies of those killed at the Korana bridge being taken away. The witness is familiar with this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My brother-in-law was killed, was among those killed here. Gojkovic Svetozar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We skipped over a part of it I think superfluous, and I would like you to pay attention to the footage that will follow, and I will have some questions for you. Please pay attention to the injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, before you proceed, I would like confirmation of the name of the place where this incident took place and to confirm the bridge that you spoke of, because there seemed to be two different spellings and places referred to. Could we get it on the record correctly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you just heard the Honourable Judge Nosworthy. Can you tell us once again where this incident happened, on which bridge in the vicinity of which town or village?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It was the bridge on the Korana river, on the left bank of the Korana river, close to the Korana Hotel in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's Croatian territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I think we have seen enough. I would like to stop this footage now and ask you, as a human being and as an experienced professional soldier who took part in the war, can you tell us how these soldiers died? You saw the injuries on them. What can we conclude on the basis of their injuries?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I know quite a lot, because my job was precisely to collect material about those extremists. In fact, I've been collecting it of my own accord and I published already one book and another one is in preparation, and another reason why I know a lot about it is that my brother-in-law, Svetozar Gojkovic, was among those killed. My sister and their child are now living in Belgrade. One thing is obvious. A similar way of killing was already seen in Kordun in the Second World War, killing by knife. Knife, as the symbol of crimes committed by Croatian forces, even back then in the former independent state of Croatia and even now. It is an unprecedented massacre. Guided by the basest instincts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that these men mostly had their throats slit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let us emphasise this: These were soldiers, members of the regular Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: 13 of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. 13 killed and 19 captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And that happened on the 21st September 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: At that time the JNA was still the legal regular armed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation I would like to tender this video clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You spoke a moment ago, Mr. Peric, about the illegal arming of certain segments of population in Croatia, about illegal arms imports, and in this connection I would like to show you a document. Can I have Defence Exhibit 107 shown. Can you read for us the first page of this document, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: This comes from the federal secretary for foreign affairs, addressed to -- this is in fact addressed to the federal foreign secretary by the federal secretary of the national defence. "We hereby send you a brief about the illegal import of weapons by an aircraft of the Uganda company and the related events," signed Colonel Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It was an aircraft called Kikas that landed on the Zagreb airport called Pleso bringing 5.000 or so pieces of infantry weapons, namely automatic rifles, SAR 80. That weaponry was seized. It had been originally sent to Croatia for its own needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number 927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I will show you another document, a 65 ter number 116. Is it in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see from this document who drafted it and to whom it was sent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's from the office of the federal secretary for national defence, sent to the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Luka Babic -- sorry, Bebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What is it about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I can read it. "Further to our telephone conversation, we hereby inform you of the number of JNA members who were illegally arrested and taken away, we do not know where, by the members of the MUP and the ZNG of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: May I please tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I'm particularly familiar with the removal of soldiers from trains carrying weapons and equipment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which soldiers were later taken away.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this become exhibit number 928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Perovic. Witness, when we are tendering documents into evidence, please hold on with your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said you served in Zagreb until the 17th of August, 1991. Why did you leave Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I certainly didn't leave of my own will. I received orders from the command when part of the command crew was being moved to the military training grounds in Slunj and two-thirds of the command remained in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of the JNA officers from the command of the 5th Army District remain in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Most of them did. Two-thirds of the personnel of the JNA remained, whereas one-third was transferred to the forward command post led by the commander, then Colonel Zivota Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where is Slunj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Slunj is to the south-west of Zagreb, about 100 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia, on the border between Kordun and Lika areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who is the commander at this Slunj forward command post, your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior chief of the -- chief of operations and training was then Major General Petar Stipetic, and the army commander, as I said before, was Colonel General Zivota Avramovic, and his deputy, Dobrasin Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in General Stipetic. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat, a native of Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's enough, thank you. Stipetic came with you to the forward command post in Slunj, and how long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. He arrived with me on the 17th. We were at Slunj at 7.00 a.m. On the 23rd of August, he said goodbye to us and left for Zagreb. I said, meaning it as a joke, why are you saying goodbye? You are coming back, aren't you? And he answered, well, that's a big question. You see that generals are being replaced overnight by a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment. He didn't come back, did he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Major General Trajce Krstavski took over from him, who had been Chief of Staff in the 13th Rijeka Corps until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: A Macedonian. And he was arrested by the Croatian armed forces near Gospic. Somebody from the top interceded and he was released, after which he became my immediate superior, chief of operations and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: After the transfer of the -- after the relocation of the forward command post to Mount Kozara, around the 20th November he left, taking purportedly sick leave to go to Macedonia and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned that in the beginning of the November 1991 you moved the forward command post from Slunj to Mount Kozara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where is Mount Kozara? I mean where in the republic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It's now in the territory of Republic of Srpska, south of the Sava River on the axis Prejador towards Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The famous celebrated Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You remained on Mount Kozara until when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Until the 27th November when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the year always.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: 27th November 1991. And then I was appointed with another two officers, to a team that was to take charge of the relocation to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why were the personnel and equipment of the 5th Army District moving to the headquarters of the 4th Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: From what I know, a reorganisation of the armed forces was going on at the time which implied the abolishing of the 7th Army District based in Sarajevo, whereas the command of the 5th Army District in Zagreb was renamed 2nd Army District and practically took over the area of responsibility and the jurisdiction of the former 7th Army District.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In which former Yugoslav republic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In the then Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When was the relocation completed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The part of the command that was on the forward command post in Kozara was relocated immediately on the 29th November 1991 to Sarajevo. While the two-thirds of the command that had remained in Zagreb under blockade had to leave Zagreb pursuant to an agreement, and on the 4th of December I met them in Sarajevo. The 4th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: All the officers of the JNA who were moved from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, were they all of the same ethnicity, or were there different ethnicities among them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: There were different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you cite an example involving a senior officer who was not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Colonel Zeljko Kordic, was a Croat and he was an officer in charge of fire guidance. Aiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other ones?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch on the mic, I did not hear his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Klastic [phoen], who completed the academy with me, he came to Sarajevo instead of Trajce Krstavski, who was the former chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Josip Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Josip Ivanovic was a Croat. He was the head of office of the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And did you know Colonel Katalina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Up until the 29th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Whereupon you went, where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Whereupon I went to western Slovenia in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When was the forward command post at Manjaca closed down?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of January, 1992 I went to Manjaca, and sometime in the month of February, 23rd or 24th of February, the Manjaca forward command post of the JNA was closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the course of February and March 1992, were there any conflicts, any flashes in Bosnia and Herzegovina and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but I believe it was the 23rd of March or the 20th when General Prascevic, the Chief of Staff, asked me to bring him the map of the area of Bosanski Brod. I brought the map over to him, and he asked me to plot in the sign for conflict in the place called Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In that settlement, the Croatian paramilitary forces had attacked the Serb population, and this was the first armed action in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The action had practically been organised in Croatia and carried out in Bosnia with a view to generating instability in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that after all of these events you went to western Slavonia. When was it that you became the chief of the zone, TO staff western Slavonia; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was western Slavonia within the area of responsibility of the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was when --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the seat of the TO zone staff, western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Okucani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about April 1992. Was there a cease-fire in force in western Slavonia; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was on the 3rd January 1992 that a cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That was the cease-fire agreement in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What did this agreement provide for, in terms of western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it stipulated that the lines reached should be frozen, and that both sides, the Croat and Serb sides, should cease any fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is this the plan that is popularly called as the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Vance Plan stipulated that in the area of western Slavonia the regular JNA forces should withdraw south of the Sava River and that's to say the units of the Banja Luka Corps. The reserve forces that were present in western Slavonia were supposed to leave the area, western Slavonia was supposed to set up its own Territorial Defence, and that this area should, by the end of June 1992, be placed in the hands of UNPROFOR, Sector West. The seat of the UNPROFOR forces was in Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The area of western Slavonia, therefore, became a UN protected area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, an UNPA area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you took over the duties of the chief of the TO staff there, what did these duties include, what was your first duty and task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The first task I had was to protect the local population in the area, regardless of whether they were Croats or Serbs, from any attacks by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What were your weapons and what were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Initially, that's to say up until December 1992, the weapons the TO units had was placed in depots under the supervision of UNPROFOR, under double-lock system. Us, we the senior officers, were in civilian clothes, and we mostly dealt with the recruitment of people and bringing units up to strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that under the Vance Plan the JNA units were supposed to be withdrawn from the area, and that the withdrawal had to be completed by the end of June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Yugoslav People's Army withdraw from the area within that time-limit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was within that time-limit that it withdrew. With their departure, the area was not covered by anyone. That's why the Krajina police brigade was set up, to protect the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the UNPROFOR forces in western Slavonia; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The commander was the Indian general, Satish Nambiar, and in western Slavonia, in particular, the commander of Sector West was Argentinian commander, Zabala.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of defending western Slavonia in the event of an attack from the outside, regardless of who the attacking force is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Under the Vance Plan and pursuant to the documents we had, the safety of the western Slavonia area was guaranteed by UNPROFOR, and in the event of the Croatian forces attacking the western Slavonia area, under the agreement the JNA were supposed to become involved in defending the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when were you the chief of the zone staff of the TO of western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Until the setting up of the Krajina army on the 1st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When the army of the Serbian Krajina was set up, were you transferred to a different duty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No. I held the same duty, but I became the Chief of Staff of the 18 Corps of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who made up the 18th Corps of the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the commanding structure or the units?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I mean the corps structure.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In addition to the corps command, there were three infantry brigades with the headcount of 500 to 1.200 or 1.300 men. There were two infantry detachments numbering roughly 120 men and a few elements of artillery and a tank company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The people manning the units, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: They were mostly from western Slavonia. 95 per cent of them were from western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: With the setting up of the Serbian army of Krajina, did your method of working change?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to wear uniforms with the insignia of the RSK army, but we were not allowed to carry any weapons with long barrels. Therefore, we were allowed to carry sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The heavy weapons remained under a double-lock system in the control of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Heavy weapons artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We spoke of the cease-fire, that's to say the Vance Plan, dating from early January 1992. Can you tell us whether this cease-fire agreement was adhered to, was it violated, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It was not adhered to, even remotely, because the UN protected area was such that it did not encompass a good part of the Serb population in eastern Slavonia, especially starting from the town of Virovitica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. My question to you, Mr. Peric, was only whether the cease-fire was adhered to, whether there were any violations, and by whom. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No. There was sporadic fire and violations of the agreement by the Croatian forces and provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the Sarajevo agreement, dating from early January 1992, was another cease-fire agreement reached, and do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 29th of March, 1994, that an agreement was signed, we called it a gentlemen's agreement, concerning the separation of the two sides, Croat and Serb. Demilitarisation was carried out on both sides about a kilometre into the depth of the respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have the Defence document number 098 shown. I will have a question to put to you in connection with that. Could you please zoom in a bit. Thank you. Is this the agreement you spoke of dated 29 March 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. That's the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Please let us turn to page 2 of the agreement - or, rather, that's page 3 - in order for us to see who the signatories of the agreement are. You will be able to see that on the third page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the Croatian government it was signed by Hrvoje Sarinic; on behalf of the Krajina authorities, minister of defence Rakic signed. Then the witness and the French general Arens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Hrvoje Sarinic was the deputy prime minister in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he was the authorised negotiator on behalf of the Croatian authorities to negotiate with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason behind the signing of this agreement, if any?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The reason was that the situation on the ground forced us to sign it. Croatia was pulling in ever stronger units toward the UNPAs, carrying out the drills and building up its posts around Krajina which indicated that they intended to occupy our area by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who initiated the signing of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I think it was primarily an agreement between the UNPROFOR and the Krajina side, the Krajina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was this agreement honored?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was not honoured by Croatia. We did honour it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 929.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOPEFUL
utterances.text: Witness, I just didn't exactly understand you. I understood you saying the agreement was concluded between UNPROFOR and the Krajina. Then it was a question if Croatia would obey to that. Was it then between Croatia and Krajina? Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
