utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact, the UNPROFOR acted as a mediator in this agreement between Croatia and our authorities in Knin, so they were a mediator. Whereas the agreement was an agreement on the cessation of hostilities and cease-fire between Croatia and Krajina, with UNPROFOR acting as the guarantor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOPEFUL
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the UNPROFOR guaranteed that there would be no attack on western Slavonia. Hence my question. What can you tell us about the activities of the UNPROFOR in the period they spent in western Slavonia. During their presence in western Slavonia. What was the nature of their engagement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you at the outset the UNPROFOR did not have strong forces and they were patchy. There were three battalions from Jordan, Nepal, and Argentina. Those forces with that particular structure were completely unable to guarantee safety in western Slavonia, and I seriously doubted their capacities to defend western Slavonia from attack, if they should -- if it should happen. But I knew that it was their mandate to guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of UNPROFOR officers and soldiers to the two sides? Did they treat both sides equally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: On the official level, their conduct was correct, proper. However, from the various contacts and reports I got from my subordinate commanding officers, I became ever more convinced in my feeling that they were not there for our sake but for the sake of Croatia, and they were actually there to see to it that we become a part of Croatia. Their mandate was practically to deliver us to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of what led you to believe that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For instance, when Croatia was testing Krajina's patience, starting with the attack on the Miljevac plateau in June 1992 until the attack on Vlasenica on the 21st of January, 1993, without any energetic response, we received mobilisation orders on the 21st of January, 1993, the entire corps was to be mobilised. We tried to carry out this mobilisation. However, the west sector commander Zabala prevented us and he was accompanied by the chief of civilian affairs of the United Nations, Mr. Fischer. In that area, Croatia mobilised its forces from Gradiska, Novska, and Pakrac axes and was in a state of full combat readiness to attack us. However, Mr. Zabala emphatically opposed mobilisation of troops by our corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me interrupt you because I have to show you another document, 008. It has to be flipped, rotated in fact. This is a document of the defence, 008, it's in English. And since I suppose you don't read English, I will read it for you. And then I would have a question. The document reads: "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, Bjelovar. Dear General, this is to inform you that on the occupied area of the former Sector West, we are expecting possible activities very soon. "I recommend to you, in order to protect UNCRO units under your command, to take the necessary measures so that they assemble in safe places and withdraw to the free part of Sector West." This is the segment that is of interest to me. This document is signed by commander of the operative sector, Bjelovar, Dzanko Luka. Now, since I familiarized you with the contents of this document, can you give us your comment. What is this in fact about? What does the Commander Dzanko Luka say to the Argentinian general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: This document was sent to the Sector West headquarters. It was received at 2.30 on the 1st of May. General Matalon was informed of it. Matalon was commander of Sector West. And the Croatian brigadier general, Dzanko Luka, who by the way my was schoolmate at the military academy, was commander of the operation zone, Bjelovar, and he sent this cable in which he indicates that combat activities are about to start soon in the former sector -- I emphasise "former sector west." By implication, he treats the Sector west as non-existent at that time. Furthermore, he indicates, he hints that those combat activities will take place and that the UNPROFOR should remove their personnel from that area for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Did the UNPROFOR command inform you of this telegram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No, although they had the duty to inform me. All the more so because in 1993 General Zabala told me, "We are an army, too, and we are responsible for the safety of western Slavonia and we will provide written guarantees." Written guarantees were then required by General Novakovic, commander of the army of Serbian Krajina. And they provided guarantees of the safety of Krajina, whereas when it came to it, they didn't inform us of the upcoming attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Operation Flash. Can you tell us some more about it. When did it begin, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I would say that Operation Flash was planned by Croatia long in advance, and that according to the testimony of Croatian Janko Bobetko in his book titled "All My Battles," Operation Flash was conceived in February 1994 [as interpreted], whereas intensive work on it started in December 1994 [as interpreted]. In February 1995 the plan was fully completed and units were ready for action. On the 25th of April, General Bobetko reported to the president of Croatia, Tudjman, that units were ready for action in western Slavonia to carry out Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. This same Janko Bobetko, army general, was it the same one who in 1971 was member of the Croatian nationalist movement in Croatia and a highly ranked JNA general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So in 1971 he was doing the same thing that he continued in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. He thought in the 1990s that his time had finally come. He left his retirement, became active again, and placed himself at the disposal of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I think it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Before the break we were talking about Operation Flash. Can you tell me when exactly it commenced, if you remember, and how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Allow me first to say the following. This operation is practically the continuation of the operation from 1991 when there was an attempt in November 1991 to actually empty the area between Virovitica and Okucani of Serb population. There was the order of the Crisis Staff of -- from Pozega about the expulsion of population from 28 villages, from Bilogora and Daruvar down to the southern area, toward the Sava River. What had not been achieved in 1991, because the population of Pakrac and Okucani opposed to suffer the same fate as when there was an exodus of the population from the Bilogora area, this was the operation called Otkos, meaning mowing down, which implied terrible devastation and so on and so fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Please pause there. I asked you about Operation Flash, when it started and how long it lasted. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It started on the 1st of May, 1995, and ended on the 4th of May, although there were some actions by the Croatian army until as late as the 8th of May, 1995, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the reason that Croatia cited and which apparently prompted Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: What was cited as the reason behind the action was the opening up of the highway, or the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that as the reason for this aggression against western Slavonia, the opening you have the motorway was cited. To your knowledge, was this true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: No. This was perhaps only the motive for such an action. Even had the motorway been opened up until the start of the operation, the operation would have been carried out, because it had long been prepared and the forces were ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at Defence document 029, please. While we're waiting for the document to appear on the screen, I will tell you that this is the book by General Janko Bobetko that you mentioned, "All My Battles," that is the title of the book. You've read the book, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, in the spring of 1995, did General Bobetko have certain functions to carry out in the Croatian army and what his role was in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That would correspond to the position of the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 396 of the book in the B/C/S version, it is 1408 the number it bears. In English it's 1555. That's 1408 in the B/C/S and 1555 in English. Yes, this is what we wanted to see. That's page 396 of the book by Janko Bobetko "All my Battles."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Could it be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, the Main Staff of the Croatian army, Zagreb. The 5th of December, 1994." That's to say December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the title of the directive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "Directive, operations number 5/94 for the execution of Operation Flash 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Dated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: 5 December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's to say, six months before Operation Flash was actually carried out there was a directive in existence concerning its execution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 403 of the book, which bears the last four digits 1415 in the B/C/S, whereas in English that's 1561.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the top half of the document, could you scroll it down, please. Could you please turn to the next page. No, no, that's not it. Under the circumstances, I think that we should place this copy before the witness in order for him to read what is contained there, because obviously this isn't what we're getting on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, must we in the English go to page 1561 or must we stay at 1555?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this time I'm really not sure. It seems that the notes I made aren't right. That's why I thought it best for the witness to take a look at the document which is to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it before you, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What is the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: According to the military terminology we used, the B/C/S word would be different. It would not say "zapovijedam" but rather "naredzujem" but it means "I order." Which means that General Janko Bobetko is issuing an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When is the order dated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I can't really see. Could you please scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, for your assistance it is page 1567 in English, just if that helps you follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And it seems to be 1426 in B/C/S, page 414 of the book, isn't it? 1D00-1426.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend, Mr. Black. We have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, do you see the document now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "Class 8/95-02/03, reference number 512" --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Read the title, "I order," and who signed the order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Army General Janko Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What does this order issued by Janko Bobetko refer to? Read out paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "The forces under the command of the forward command post of the Main Staff of the Croatian army and the forward command post of the Bjelovar Military District are to be organised and the same forces should immediately proceed to liquidate the remaining enemy forces until their complete destruction or unconditional capture."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What is the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The 4th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to the second page of this document. In English it's 1.569. 1569. Mr. Peric, please read the title of the document, what it is about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: "The report of Colonel General Petar Stipetic on the implementation of the second stage of Operation Flash according to the special order by the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army, Staff General Janko Bobetko, dated 4 May 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please turn to page 398 of the book. In English the last four digits should be 1557 and in the B/C/S 1410. This is a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My page 1557 is not a map, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page of the book is 394, 394. That's supposed to be the page 394 of the book. 394 and 395. It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, again if I can be of assistance. I think, I remember from discussions with Defence counsel, that there had been a problem getting this in e-court. We do have one extra copy for the Bench if you would like to follow along that way. As far as I know, this map is not as yet up in e-court. That would be the solution I would propose. I have another copy for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. We would appreciate your copy. Mr. Perovic, would you like to see that before it comes to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what this is about, and I'm very grateful to my learned friend Mr. Black for his assistance. Could this please be shown now to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. And thank you to you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So is this an excerpt from the book? Will we have this on the screen anyway? In the B/C/S version, I mean? This is a copy from the B/C/S from the original of the book, I suppose, and we should see it on the original version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be placed on the ELMO so that the witness could follow too. This is the only copy I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But what I was asking you, Mr. Perovic, is this part of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is part of Janko Bobetko's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which page or pages of the book, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 394 and 395. The map covers the two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, please look at what the map refers to. Look at the title at the top. Could this just be scrolled up a bit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: This is an offensive operation, offensive Operation Flash, dated 1st until the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Which year? 1995? Is that what is written on the map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We don't need the map anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this book into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, can you explain us this map, pages 394 and 95 of the book, is apparently not in e-court, and is this now supposed to be an extra exhibit, and are the English parts put together as excerpts being tendered or the whole book? This would be a problem if we would have to consider it a whole book or an exhibit in the B/C/S version and only English excerpts, a few pages in the English version. Can you clarify that, please. We had that problem before, you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the map as a separate exhibit, while the remaining pages of the book we would like to tender as a separate exhibit. In fact, it seems to me simpler to make the whole book a Defence exhibit with the pages that we looked at highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's the very problem we are trying to obviate, Mr. Perovic. In the English your pages go up to 41, I can see here. In the book you have been talking about pages 300 and something. Do you really want to tender this whole book into evidence, and all of it -- are you going to translate into English all of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In fact, 460 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because it is of no use to the Bench if it is not in English. We are not going to be able to understand what is written in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that the pages we have viewed be introduced as one exhibit, and the map we have seen as another exhibit of the Defence. So I'm not trying to tender the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to the book coming in. What I would ask is that we have the opportunity to suggest other pages for translation. I think that's what was done with a couple of other books that are in evidence. We'll do that as quickly as we can. I don't frankly know how long it will take us, if we even -- I guess we have the whole book now. So subject to that condition. And also, the map, if it's going to be made an exhibit, I would ask that it -- the version from the book be admitted. The version that we saw on the ELMO is highlighted and seems to have other marks. If those are the witness's marks, then maybe he could establish that. Otherwise, I would suggest that we just use one of the other copies that is not highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with both these suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Okay. Then by agreement between the parties, the whole book is being admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what you said, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If that's what I said I didn't express myself well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you don't mind the whole book going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What I said was, and it was not very well put, is I don't object to the book coming in. And what I really meant is the excerpts that are in English, that's why I suggested that we have the chance to translate additional excerpts. I agree with what Your Honour says makes perfect sense, of course, that what is not in English is of little use to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But at the same time, if the whole book is not tendered, how are you going to go and choose your excerpts?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We will have to sit down with a language assistant, Your Honour, and try to go through the book and identify what else is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But for you to go through the book, the book you must be in evidence, shouldn't it be? Or do you have access to the book outside the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If the book remains on e-court as it is, we can access it there, or I'm sure we can come to an agreement with the Defence to look at the hard copy. So we can take care of that issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So what do you suggest be admitted into evidence in relation to the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just the excerpts in B/C/S together with the English translations. And, Your Honour, what I think we did the last time we had this problem was that the parties had a week or some amount of time, and we even did a little annex that said this ERN range in B/C/S matches this ERN range in English. We can do that so that what is admitted is in both languages but it is still only the excerpts that are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you now on the wavelength with your learned friend, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. In that event, then, that Exhibit 931 must be withdrawn. Only the excerpts that Defence counsel referred to in B/C/S together with the equivalent English translations are admitted into evidence, and may they place be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the excerpts of the book will become exhibit number 931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the map at page 394 to 395 of the book is also admitted into evidence. May it also be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become exhibit number 932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm being advised by Judge Hoepfel that, Mr. Perovic, if the B/C/S and the English versions can be correlated so that it is understood which section relates to which section in the other language. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you said a moment ago that not for a moment did you believe the reason put forward by the Croatian side to justify the aggression in the form of Operation Flash. In this connection, let me show you parts of the record from the extraordinary meeting of the Defence Council and Security Council of Croatia of the 29th of April, 1995. That is 028 on the 65 ter list. And the pages I want to show is marked 4790, those are the last digits of the number of the B/C/S version. Page 4790, please in B/C/S. Last digits 4790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, may I ask you to refer to the line where the witness said, as we said a moment ago that not for a moment ... and so on. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the second session, I asked the witness, what was the reason, according to the Croatian version, for Operation Flash, and they said it was to open the highway, the motorway, and then the witness expressed his doubts that this was indeed the real reason, and that's what I referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't remember him having said "not for a moment" they believed that, or he believed that. This is what you said now, this was your interpretation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allow the possibility that I maybe read more into his words than he actually said on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is not the first time. Please try to be very exact when helping the witness to go on with his statements without leading him or interpreting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed if you can give us the page number in the English version, please, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This entire document has been translated, but at this moment I really can't say with any certainty under what number this page is recorded in the English version. If you -- with your leave, I can show this document to the witness and as soon as possible we will provide the translation of this particular page or indicate where it is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour. And I believe that it's at 1D001065, but of course I don't know, because I don't speak B/C/S, but that's my guess, based on what I can see on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We do have 1065 on the screen. Mr. Perovic, proceed. We will assume that we are in the right place until the contrary is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is part of the transcript. On this page the people who speak are Hrvoje Sarinic, Miroslav Tudjman, the president, meaning Franjo Tudjman, and then again Hrvoje Sarinic speaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And at the top we also have Nikica Valentic, although he doesn't speak too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it's in the English version. The layout in B/C/S is a bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Hrvoje Sarinic says: "All right. But they said they would open up this thing, so as soon as they assess that the situation has calmed down, that's probably going to be today. Serbs would lift their concrete pyramids that they had placed and the other side would remove their trucks." Miroslav Tudjman says: Let them open it, but we will rechannel traffic even before so that they don't use that road, and we'll explain it by saying that it's not safe." President: "No, no. Send a couple of policemen in mufti and soldiers to first observe and then to cause an incident." And Hrvoje Sarinic says to that: "Strategically speaking, it's better for us to open the motorway, but politically it's not so good, because we will be moving into action after it has already been opened." Would you comment on this discussion of the Council for Defence and National Security of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely the confirmation of my doubts that their action was precipitated by the closing of our motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you another document. It's the transcript from a session of the same council, held on the 30th of April, 1995, chaired by Dr. Franjo Tudjman. That's Defence exhibit 108.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before we move on, Your Honour, I just note this hasn't been -- the document we were looking at hasn't been put into evidence, and I wonder if Defence counsel wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just was going to ask what Defence counsel wants to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am tendering this as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the document is admitted into evidence as an Defence exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 933.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You said you wanted to put another document. Thank you, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the other document. My associates tell me that there's something wrong with it in e-court. Therefore, we prepared, just in case, the English translation of the transcript of this session, and may I have it distributed now. I don't know if the Prosecutor has a copy. The document should be available in e-court, but an associate told me that something is wrong with at least a part of it; that's why we prepared a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I do have a copy, and this is in response to something I had noticed, that the translation in e-court only contains I think the first 10 pages, whereas I assume the translation which has just been handed out is the complete translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black, and thank you, Mr. Perovic. And, Mr. Black, you don't mind the handing out of this document to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic, just from my curiosity, how much longer are you going to be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the pages 4830 and 4831 of the minutes be shown. This is the version in the B/C/S. Perhaps my learned friend Mr. Black will be of assistance again, because I don't have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm afraid you overestimate me. I haven't found it, but I will be looking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Rather over than under, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 4830 and 31 of the minutes are the ones I'm looking for. I am quite certain of the abilities of my learned friend. I'm sure he'll be of assistance, with the version in the English, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, my best is that that is on page 9 of the translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. What could we do without you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much to my colleague, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's page 4830 in the B/C/S. And the participants in this part of the discussion at the session are Mladen Markac, President Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Petar Stipetic. And I will read the part uttered by president. It is implied that this -- this is President Tudjman. "Yes, of course, that is what I said. That's quite clear. That's why you know even with two cars," and so on. Gojko Susak goes on to say, I quote: "Mladen, where would be the easiest, where would it be easier to do that? "President: Listen. To fire upon our car, well, and then here they shot our car. Of course there would be two cars. They opened fire. So that, you know, the war is a measure of fairness. All is fair in a war. "Petar Stipetic: Even if there are eight of them dead and four were reported, if really eight of them were dead, then it should be stated that four of them were killed in the provocation, provide the names of the people killed and so on, and then issue a release and carry that further, if it's a provocation and so on and so forth." At page 4831 of the same transcript, Mladen Markac goes on to say: "This is to open the road. We will create the incident. We will mount the incident and use it after the operation." Then President Tudjman goes on to say: "This would be the cue for the Jordanians to take cover." The last page of the transcript in the B/C/S version, 4852 is the number, Gojko Susak says, and I quote: "Very well. That won't have that much of an effect. UNPROFOR will deal with that." President goes on to say: "Wait a minute. The Argentinians are there." Someone intervenes from side. "The Argentinians are up there and down there are the Jordanians. Very well then. Try and persuade the Argentinians and the Jordanians to lie low for a while, to take a nap." Gojko Susak goes on to say: Plesna is on good terms particularly for the Argentinians, and as for the Jordanians, we'll see about that." Mr. Peric, you heard the conversation which took place at the -- one of the sessions of this council. What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: This confirms what I knew, and that was that the incident on the motorway, between the 28 and 29th of April, was engineered by Croatia, because I know for a fact I was there on the motorway after Tihomir Blagovic [phoen] had been killed by knife in Gradiska. I spent that entire night on the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document numbered 108 as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 934.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I will show you a Defence document, the number is 012. That's the document. Could you please zoom in a bit. Mr. Peric, the document is in English. As you do not speak English, I will read it out for you. "Statement by Yasushi Akashi, Special Representative of the Secretary-General. Despite the agreement reached on the 3rd of May, 1995, for a complete cessation of hostilities, I am gravely concerned that there was still fighting today in a few areas, including near Pakrac, and continued tensions and threatening actions in the cease-fire areas in all Sectors." As you're able to see, at the bottom of the document, there is the date and hours, 8.00 p.m., on the 4th of May, 1995. What can you tell us about this document? How would you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the statement. Apparently Mr. Akashi also took a nap. On the 2nd of May, the Croatian forces entered western Slovenia and violated the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender the document and can it be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number 935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in these events in western Slovenia throughout the duration of Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To the extent you remember, can you tell us what the consequences of Operation Flash were.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: The consequences lay primarily in the fact that in an area of 507 square kilometres, and that is the area of western Slovenia, with two echelons of the Croatian army, 18.000 was the first echelon and 35.000 numbered the second echelon, the Croatian army was pitted against 4.000 strong poorly armed citizens who were actually citizens of their own country. In a bit less than 36 hours, western Slavonia was cleared of its population and part of its population was massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many people were killed in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Although we have rough figures and they stated there were 284 persons, persons we know -- whose names we know, I believe that the total of the persons killed in the operation was 2.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How many people, and I mean Serbs, left the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: In the population -- the entire population in the southern part of the sector and on the 1st and 2nd May, some parts of the population from the northern part. In total, 20.000 persons. Out of the 283 persons who were killed and whose names we know, 77 of them were elderly, around 30 of them were women, and around ten of them were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the OTP at a certain point concerning the consequences of Operation Flash, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in 2002 that I gave a statement in the case against the Croatian general Markac. There were two investigators. I believe one was from Sri Lanka and the other one from Ukraine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was it the 20th of February or the 4th of April of 2002?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the premises of Veritas that I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give any documents to the investigators on that occasion which had to do with Operation Flash and its consequences?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I believe I did. I gave a tape of an intercepted conversation between members of the Croatian army in the northern part of Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the fact that someone on the Croatian side had been prosecuted for the crimes committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody has been prosecuted to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. When we spoke of the mass consider at the Korana bridge, I forgot to ask you the following. Who carried out this action or, rather, who committed the crime? Was the person who committed the crime identified?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It was a person, a certain person named Hrastov, who was purportedly brought to trial but was then released because of lack of evidence apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This person's name is Hrastov. You say that he was tried but that he was acquitted because of lack of evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he constitutes a national hero of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that he is in the national hero of Croatia [as interpreted]. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: It means that he is a highly respected citizen of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether President Tudjman decorated this person at some point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my examination-in-chief, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric -- actually, could we lower the ELMO so the witness and I have a clear view of one another, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, my name is Colin Black. As you've probably gathered, I'm one of the Prosecutors working on this case, and I will have a few questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You served your entire career in the Yugoslav army, and you were -- is it fair to say you were proud of your service in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you were proud of what you thought it stood for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. And my question was whether you were proud of what you thought the JNA stood for. And I just explain by saying before the 1990s and certainly under Tito, I think in your words you said that the JNA was a hotbed of Yugoslav sentiment. It was kind of supposed to be an example of unity and brotherhood in Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you were proud to be part of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So when ethnic divisions arose, you found that to be upsetting, is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: You could put it that way, upsetting, and there was a feeling of anticipation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And was that true about, you know, ethnic hostilities or sort of nationalism on all sides, or was it just in Croatia and Slovenia that that upset you, or was it a reaction that you had against all kinds of ethnic extremism?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: From 1980 onwards, that is after Tito's death, we, in the army, professionals at least, could feel that in the units stationed in Croatia and Slovenia, some strange things were happening. Something was going on in the top echelons but also on the ground, and there was something strange about the functioning of the system of command and control. And if you want me, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, if you could just briefly explain what you mean.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the staffing policy. After Tito's death, skills and qualifications and professionalism didn't matter that much anymore. The system of ethnic representation became much more important in appointment to senior duties. And JNA units, as a whole, started downsizing, especially in Croatia. So we have the entire basin of Kordun and Lika almost empty, without any units. We had one unit in Petrinja and one in Karlovac, the rest of the territory was covered by echelon B, that is the reserve corps. No live units, as we called them. And then another thing, on the level of operational strategic units some kind of grouping started; namely, the tendency was for the whole commanding personnel to be chosen from the natives of that area, like Croats around Zagreb, Muslims around Sarajevo, et cetera, which I don't think was a good thing. Third, some bizarre requests were put forward; we thought them very unusual. Through a publication called Mladina, Slovenes started demanding that the Slovene language be used in the JNA in Slovenia, that Slovenes, Slovene recruits no longer be sent outside Slovenia to do their military service, and the whole army started ripping at the ethnic seams. To us, at the lower operational tactical level, it was impossible to understand how the superior command was allowing those things to happen, especially after the dissolution began, after the 14th party congress. It became obvious that all the new processes that were going on in the society were going to be echoed in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And following on from what you've just told us, is it right that certainly some people, and maybe especially the leadership in Croatia and Slovenia, had a slightly different view of the JNA, that they were more suspicious of the JNA than of course you were, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what, I am an amateur historian, and I think that that was the third betrayal. Slovenes and Croats took advantage of Yugoslavia when it was useful to them, and when it was no longer useful, they turned their backs on it. The same goes for the army. The only -- the only part of the former Yugoslavia that welcomed Hitler's troops were Croats, throwing flowers on them. And you could expect it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: -- you could kind of expect this sort of behaviour on their part when the dissolution began, if we are going to learn any history lessons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but I don't think we need to go down a general history. But just before we break for the day, if you could answer my question, please, whether or not it's correct that the leadership at least and some of the people in Slovenia and Croatia had a different view of the JNA than what you did, that they were distrustful of the JNA, or maybe saw the JNA as not representing their own interests. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Well, you told me to forget history, but history is the teacher of life and we could learn something from it. Unless we learn those lessons, everything that has already happened will happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: For the fact that they viewed it differently --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you to forget history, but here we're focussed on a certain specific topic. So you were just about -- I think you had started to answer my question, it is about how the JNA was viewed in Slovenia and Croatia. Just please finish that and we will break for the day.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: We, the professional military men, officers and soldiers, saw how we were treated and viewed by the official authorities, not by the people. Of course it's up to them to have their views, but to us it was unacceptable. Their behaviour was geared at breaking up Yugoslavia, and it was an attack on the JNA from the moment Demos won in Slovenia and HDZ won in Croatia, they called us Serbo-Chetniks, Yugo-Chetniks, et cetera. Whereas the army was genuinely a popular army. The army built more infrastructure, more water supplier lines and other infrastructure in both Croatia and Slovenia than civilian authorities ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So in short, yes, the JNA was viewed differently, at least by the leadership in Croatia and Slovenia, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC
utterances.text: Correct. They viewed us as the hostile army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that is a good point to stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are adjourned for the day and reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
